about_what_body: File Time Cluster groups the photos and videos in one folder into events, using the date and time written in each filename. Each event can then be moved into its own folder, numbered in chronological order.
about_how_body:
1. Click “Choose folder…” and pick the folder that holds the files.
2. The events appear right away: on the to-scale timeline at the top, in the calendar, and in the cluster list. Nothing has been moved yet.
3. Click a day in the calendar, or anywhere on the timeline, to see that day hour by hour with every file listed. Click a bar or a row in the cluster list to jump to that event.
4. The boundary between events is learned from the timestamps in this folder. A frequent photographer and an occasional one get different boundaries. Nothing is read from the pictures themselves. Click “Update preview” after changing the safety limits.
5. Click “Apply clustering” to create the folders and move the files. You are asked to confirm first. The timeline, calendar, and cluster list stay as they are until you choose another folder.
6. Copy more photos into the same folder later, then click “Update preview”. Photos already in event folders are included. A new photo joins an existing event when the pause is short enough, or starts a new event when it is not. Apply then moves only the files that need a different folder, and renames an event folder whose times changed.
7. Click “Flatten clustering” to move those files back into the chosen folder and remove the event folders. Other subfolders are left alone.
8. Use the Language menu to show this window in English, Hindi, Marathi, German, French, Japanese, or Korean.
about_views_body:
Timeline: one bar per event, drawn to scale, with a tick for every file underneath. Use −, + and Fit, or Ctrl/Cmd with the mouse wheel, to zoom. The plain wheel scrolls sideways.
Calendar: days with files are coloured and show the event number (#) and file count. Paler days sit inside a multi-day event but have no files. ◀ and ▶ move one month; ◀◀ and ▶▶ jump to the previous or next month that has files.
Day detail: the chosen day from 00:00 to 24:00, with its files and the event each belongs to.
about_names_body:
An event on one calendar day:  1 24-11-2015 10.01.25 to 18.50.08
An event across several days:  2 09-11-2015 20.49.41 to 12-11-2015 10.24.42
The leading number keeps the folders in chronological order.
about_files_body:
Files sitting directly in the chosen folder are clustered, and so are photos already inside event folders from an earlier Apply. Other subfolders are never entered. Files whose names carry no timestamp stay where they are and are listed in the Skipped tab. Existing files are never overwritten.
Recognised names include IMG_20240101_101500.jpg, VID_20240101_101500.mp4, PANO_…, 20240101101500123.jpg, Screenshot_2024-01-01-10-15-00.png, IMG-20240101-WA0001.jpg (taken as midnight), CamScanner 01-02-2024 10.15.pdf and 13-digit Unix millisecond stamps.
about_options_body:
The app fits two patterns to the pauses in the chosen folder: short pauses inside an event, and long pauses between events. The boundary is where a pause looks more like the long pattern. It is learned again for every folder, from timestamps only. Pictures themselves are never read.
Never split before (default 3 h) and always split after (default 720 h) are safety limits around that learned boundary.
The learned boundary is saved in filetimecluster-model.json in the chosen folder, next to the files, where you can open it. It is reused when a later batch is too small to fit a new one.
Minimum and maximum year (defaults 1990 and 2100): a stamp outside this window is ignored.
Clock, epoch and date priority (defaults 30, 20 and 10): when one filename matches more than one pattern, the higher number wins. A tie keeps the match that starts earlier in the name.
Filename patterns: the regular expressions used to read a time from a name. They start out as the built-in ones. Clear a box to turn that pattern off, or replace it. A clock pattern needs the groups y, mo, d, h, mi and s. The day-month clock needs a, b, y, h and mi. Unix milliseconds needs ms. A date needs y, mo and d. Then click “Update preview”.
